title: Medtronic plc, Q2 2027 Earnings Call, Nov 24, 2026

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Good morning, and welcome to our fiscal '27 second quarter earnings webcast. I'm Ingrid Goldberg, Head of Medtronic Investor Relations. And I'm joined by Geoff Martha, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; and Thierry Pieton, Chief Financial Officer. Geoff and Thierry will provide comments on the results of our second quarter, which ended on October 30, 2026, and our outlook for the remainder of fiscal '27. After our prepared remarks, we'll take questions from the sell-side analysts that cover the company.

Earlier this morning, we issued a press release discussing our quarterly results and several financial schedules. We also posted an earnings presentation that provides additional details on our performance. The presentation can be accessed in our earnings press release and on our website at investorrelations.medtronic.com. During today's program, many of our statements will be forward-looking, and actual results may differ materially as explained in our SEC filings. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statements. Unless otherwise stated, all comparisons are on a year-over-year basis and revenue comparisons are made on an organic basis, which excludes the impact of foreign currency.

First quarter revenue in the current and prior year reported as Other as well as significant acquisitions, divestitures or other significant discrete items. The quarterly results we are reporting today reflect the consolidation of the Diabetes business through October 15 when we completed the split-off of our remaining interest in the MiniMed Group to Medtronic shareholders. Reconciliations of all non-GAAP financial measures can be found in our earnings press release or on our website at investorrelations.medtronic.com. And finally, our EPS guidance does not include any charges or gains that will be reported as non-GAAP adjustments to earnings during the fiscal year. With that, I'm now pleased to hand it over to Geoff.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Okay. Thanks, Ingrid, and good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us.

Q2 was another strong, consistent quarter for Medtronic. We delivered 6.5% organic revenue growth, demonstrating that the changes we're making across strategy, operations and culture are translating into results. Look, we are executing. We're advancing meaningful innovation and actively shaping our portfolio in markets where Medtronic can lead and create the most value. Now the broader medtech landscape is complex and has been uneven with variability by procedure, by geography and product category.

We continue to closely monitor these dynamics, but our Q2 performance demonstrates that we are in resilient end markets and executed well despite these pressure points. Here, the breadth and the depth of the Medtronic portfolio is an important advantage. We have strong positions in good markets, anchored by a healthy base of large leading franchises. We have new growth drivers that are scaling due to our differentiated innovation. And we continue to invest in our pipeline, both organically and through disciplined M&A and venture investing. Our teams are focused on what we can control, consistently executing to deliver on our commitments. In addition to the strength of our Q2 performance, I'm even more excited about the important milestones that we achieved this quarter. And look, the list is long, but I want to highlight a few things.

First, new clinical evidence for Symplicity, Category I CPT codes for both Symplicity and Altaviva, completion of Sphere-360 U.S. trial enrollment and multiple regulatory approvals in ENT and importantly, 2 for Hugo, including general surgery procedures. These milestones are critical because they strengthen our foundation for durable performance over the long term. And we're going to have more -- much more to share at our Investor Day on December 10 and 11, which is just 2 weeks away.

But for today, I'm going to stay focused on the quarter. So with that, let's dive into Q2. Our largest franchises, CRM, CST and Surgical continue to deliver durable growth while newer platforms are becoming more meaningful contributors. This includes continued performance from CAS and Pelvic Health and building momentum across Coronary, Peripheral Vascular and the strength in ACM. Now Cardiovascular was up 10.4% in the quarter, and this year's TCT medical conference was a notable highlight, including positive late-breaking data from the Spyral AFFIRM trial, which demonstrated significant blood pressure reductions starting at just 6 months.

This includes an 18-point reduction in in-office systolic blood pressure. AFFIRM also demonstrated consistent blood pressure reductions across diverse patient populations, including Black and Hispanic patients, women, patients over 65 and those with type 2 diabetes and reduced kidney function.

Look, this AFFIRM data, it validates Symplicity's use in real-world practice and underscore both the rapid and widespread clinical impact of this procedure. In Cardiac Ablation Solutions, we delivered another strong quarter, growing 58% globally and gaining another 7 points of share year-over-year in the U.S. Our confidence in Affera continues with the consistent performance of Sphere-9 alongside our advancing pipeline.

Enrollment in the U.S. pivotal trial for Sphere-360 is now complete and has entered its 12-month follow-up period ahead of the PMA submission. Look, our CAS team continues to execute at a high level, expanding into new indications into new geographies and while building out a competitive and comprehensive EP platform. This platform spans mapping, focal and single-shot ablation, software and ICE technology. All of this, we are confident that our CAS journey is far from over.

Now pivoting to neuroscience. Our CST franchise was also a highlight, delivering another 6% quarter, driven by high single-digit performance in neurosurgery and the Stealth AXiS global launch. Now even as the rollout remains in early stages, Stealth AXiS is beginning to contribute meaningfully as adoption expands. In the U.S., we delivered mid-single-digit core Spine and Biologics growth and low double-digit Neurosurgery growth, reflecting continued share gains.

In Medical Surgical, we delivered a strong quarter, delivering more than 4%. This quarter, we achieved 2 important regulatory milestones for Hugo, FDA clearance for multiple general surgery procedures and for LigaSure RAS. All these approvals, they matter. The general surgery indication significantly expands where Hugo can compete, particularly in multi-quadrant and hernia surgeries that benefit the most from the platform's modularity. And LigaSure brings one of our most trusted advanced energy technologies to our robotics platform. We also continue to make progress expanding Hugo into additional indications.

For GYN, we recently completed a human factor study and expect to submit these additional data to the FDA early next calendar year. In robotics, we remain focused on system performance, expanding indications, growing utilization and giving customers choice, choice across the full spectrum of solutions, open, lap and robotic-assisted surgery. We also built on our disciplined portfolio strategy this quarter, adding new growth opportunities in attractive markets while refining the portfolio where it makes sense.

First, we successfully completed the separation of our Diabetes business, MiniMed. This was the largest split-off in medtech history and is a clear example of our commitment to actively shape the portfolio and focus our resources where Medtronic has the greatest impact. This split was a significant accomplishment for both teams, and we look forward to MiniMed's continued success as a stand-alone company.

This quarter, we also announced our intention to acquire Contego Medical, following their recent FDA approval for the Neuroguard IEP Direct System, which is the first and only TCAR system with integrated embolic protection. TCAR offers a less invasive alternative to open carotid surgery while avoiding the aortic arch. This reduces stroke risk during the procedure. This differentiated technology complements our existing capabilities in Peripheral Vascular, which is a large and attractive market growing double digits.

While these are different transactions, MiniMed and Contego reflect the same disciplined strategy. We are actively shaping the portfolio towards the company's strengths and putting capital where we see the best returns. So we made real progress this quarter, building an even stronger foundation for the future. Our largest franchises, they performed well. Newer growth platforms continue to scale, and we advanced important innovation across the portfolio.

At Investor Day, we'll give you a much more comprehensive view of where Medtronic is headed, where we're investing and how we expect to translate those opportunities into durable growth and value creation. With that, I'll turn it over to Thierry to take you through our business performance, financial results and outlook in more detail. Thierry?

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Thanks, Geoff, and hello, everyone. To begin, just a quick note on MiniMed. As you know, we completed the separation with 2 weeks remaining in the quarter. Our reported P&L includes diabetes through the separation date. Diabetes revenue is reported in Other and is excluded from our organic revenue growth rate for the full quarter. With that context, revenue this quarter was $9.4 billion, representing a reported growth of 4.5% and organic growth of 6.5%. The U.S. grew 8% and international 5%.

Starting in Cardiovascular, the portfolio delivered 10% revenue growth in the second quarter. Electrophysiology Therapies, or EPT, grew 19%. Within EPT, Cardiac Ablations was again a significant contributor, delivering 58% growth, including 80% in the U.S., where we continue to gain share rapidly. In Q3, we continue to expect to grow approximately 2.5x the market growth rate.

Cardiac Rhythm Management was up 8% and gained another 80 basis points of global share. Defibrillation Solutions performance was supported by growth in EV ICD and the OmniaSecure CSP lead, while Cardiac Pacing Therapies was driven by low 20s growth in Micra.

Moving to Interventional Cardiology Therapies or ICT. Performance in the quarter was flat globally. Coronary and renal denervation grew high single digits. Coronary grew mid-single digits, including a nearly 300 basis point contribution from CathWorks. We're also pleased with the new CMS payment pathway, which will take effect in January 2027, further expanding access to CathWorks FFRangio and supporting less invasive coronary assessment.

In Ardian, we continue to make progress on reimbursement, market development and pipeline. This quarter, we received Category I CPT code approval, an important validating milestone for Symplicity. The new codes take effect in January 2028, establishing physician reimbursement and opening new commercial coverage conversations. Our transradial Spyral+ catheter also remains on track for launch later this fiscal year, bringing Ardian into a familiar physician workflow with the majority of U.S. PCIs now performed transradially.

Structural Heart declined mid-single digits with U.S. procedure volumes stable since last May. There's more work to do here, and we continue to invest meaningfully behind this business, including the inorganic investments made in Anteris and Pi-Cardia, alongside our internal mitral and tricuspid programs. Earlier this month at TCT, we also presented baseline characteristics from our ongoing EXPAND II trial evaluating TAVR in patients with moderate aortic stenosis.

Closing out the portfolio, Cardiovascular Surgery grew 2% globally and Peripheral Vascular Health was up 4%. Moving now to Neuroscience, which grew 3% worldwide, including 4% in the U.S. Cranial & Spinal Technologies delivered 6% growth, led by high single-digit growth in Neurosurgery with continued ramp from Stealth AXiS now in its second full quarter since launch. We also completed our first Stealth AXiS cases in Europe, expanding the platform globally. In the U.S., Core Spine and Biologics delivered mid-single-digit growth as we continue to take share.

Specialty Therapies grew 2%. Within Specialty, Neurovascular grew low single digits. Hemorrhagic grew low single digits globally and high single digits in the U.S., driven by pipeline for flow diversion, Artisse and the launch of Onyx 12 for MMAe. Scientia also had a strong first full quarter following the acquisition, contributing more than 8 points of inorganic growth to Neurovascular. Pelvic Health delivered mid-single-digit growth as strong performance from Altaviva more than offset broader SNM market softness. Here as well, we continue to gain share. We also achieved Category I CPT approval for Altaviva, effective January 2028, and an important validation of its clinical value that extends site of care options and materially broadens the commercial opportunity.

ENT grew low single digits worldwide, driven by high single-digit growth in the U.S. We are also now bringing AiBLE to ENT, connecting more technology, data and workflow to create a more integrated and differentiated ecosystem. Neuromodulation declined 2%, reflecting the current SCS market environment and DBS replacement headwinds. SPR Therapeutics delivered a strong early performance in temporary peripheral nerve stimulation with revenue exceeding our expectations in its first full quarter following the acquisitions and adding 5 points of inorganic revenue growth.

Medical Surgical had another strong quarter at 4% global growth, including 7% in the U.S. Surgical revenue increased 3%, led by performance in the U.S. We saw strength in Advanced Energy and Wound Management, driven by share gains from our LigaSure vessel sealing and V-Loc barbed sutures. We're excited to have received clearances for LigaSure RAS and multiple general surgery procedures for Hugo. Both are important milestones that support our continued momentum as we expand the U.S. launch.

Endoscopy grew mid-single digits, supported by continued momentum across Endoflip 300 and Nexpowder. Last but not least, Acute Care & Monitoring was a meaningful contributor to growth again, up 8%, including 12% in the U.S. with broad-based strength across the business. We expect growth to moderate in the back half due to stronger comps.

With that, I'll turn to the P&L and some of the key drivers of our performance this quarter. Our adjusted gross margin was 65%. We maintained discipline on pricing, which provided a 20 basis point benefit in the quarter. Net of inflation, cost down was flat. This is in part due to timing, and we expect our COGS efficiency programs to provide a net benefit to gross margin for the full fiscal year. Mix was unfavorable in Q2 by 60 basis points. As in prior quarters, the Diabetes business and CAS mix continue to impact gross margin in the near term. However, CAS mix reflects our strong commercial momentum as our expanding installed base builds our foundation for higher-margin catheter pull-through over the long term. Mix this quarter was also pressured by softness in Structural Heart and Neuromodulation, both higher-margin businesses.

The tariff-related impact was slightly positive as tariffs paid were offset by the related refunds. And finally, foreign exchange had an 80 basis point negative impact. Adjusted SG&A grew 6% and was 33.2% of revenue. We continue to invest behind our highest priority growth opportunities and are integrating recent acquisitions while using AI and digitization to drive efficiency and create capacity.

Adjusted R&D was 7.8% of revenue in Q2. Organic innovation remains at the foundation of our growth and a core strength of Medtronic, particularly in large complex markets as we're seeing with CRM, Stealth AXiS and Altaviva. And we're now complementing that with targeted M&A, adding new technologies and expanding our opportunity. We announced our agreement to acquire Contego last week, and the acquisitions already in the portfolio are delivering strong results. We now expect SPR Therapeutics and Scientia to contribute more than $175 million of inorganic revenue in fiscal year '27. Their contribution will move to organic revenue in the first quarter of next fiscal year.

Our adjusted operating profit was $2.2 billion, up 1% year-over-year. Adjusted operating margin was 23.4%. Our adjusted tax rate was 19.9%, 220 basis points higher than expected and up 350 basis points year-over-year. This was driven primarily by the reassessment of our income tax reserves, and we do not expect it to reoccur.

All in all, our adjusted EPS was $1.34 at the high end of our guidance range and ahead of Street expectations. This is despite the $0.02 negative impact from the timing of the MiniMed separation. Now turning to our outlook for the balance of the year. On the top line, we delivered a strong second quarter and continue to expect fiscal year '27 organic revenue growth of 7.25% to 7.75%.

This translates to approximately 2.5% growth on a reported basis post MiniMed split. We are maintaining this range while absorbing the approximately 20 basis points impact from the loss of Diabetes business organic revenue growth. While our performance gives us confidence, we also recognize that the environment continues to evolve and our year-over-year comps in key categories get harder in the second half. In the third quarter, we're expecting roughly 5% organic revenue growth, translating into down roughly 3.8% on a reported basis.

Based on recent FX rates, we expect foreign exchange to be roughly a $40 million to $140 million headwind for the full year with an approximate $20 million to $70 million headwind in the third quarter. We believe this outlook reflects the strength that we're seeing in the business and our confidence in our ability to execute through the remainder of the year.

Moving down the P&L and starting with gross margin. We continue to make good progress in pricing and our COGS efficiency initiatives. We also keep investing with discipline in R&D and SG&A, directing resources towards our highest priority growth opportunities to support durable, sustainable revenue growth over the long term. Taken together, we expect fiscal year '27 operating profit growth of roughly 6% despite the loss of operating profit from the Diabetes business and approximately 90 basis points of operating margin expansion.

For the remainder of the fiscal year, we expect the impact of MiniMed separation on earnings to be roughly offset by the benefit from the lower share count. As a reminder, the share count retirement reduces our fiscal year '27 share count by 31 million shares with the full 55 million reflected in fiscal year '28. And finally, on EPS, we are maintaining our fiscal year '27 guidance range of $5.94 to $6. This represents 8% growth rate at the midpoint.

For the third quarter, we expect EPS of $1.40 to $1.42, which represents approximately 3.7% growth at the midpoint. We expect foreign exchange impact to be roughly neutral to EPS for both the third quarter and the full year. Look, in closing, our teams delivered another strong quarter, and I'm encouraged by the execution we continue to see across the business. We remain focused on building from here, and I look forward to providing more detail on our longer-term outlook at our upcoming Investor Day in December.
And with that, I'll turn it back to you, Geoff.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Okay. Thank you, Thierry. Q2 is another meaningful proof point of our strategy and execution translating into results. Our breadth gives us greater resilience and multiple paths to growth while allowing us to continue investing through product cycles and across our pipeline. Our priority is straightforward. Do what we said we would do, advance the pipeline, execute commercially, invest with discipline and deliver for patients, customers and shareholders. We feel good about the progress we're making while recognizing there is more work ahead. And we look forward to seeing many of you at Investor Day and going deeper on these opportunities.
With that, let's turn to Q&A. Ingrid, please provide the instructions and queue up the analysts.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: [Operator Instructions]
Finally, please be advised that this Q&A session is being recorded.
We'll take our first question from Matt O'Brien at Piper Sandler. Go ahead, Matt.

segments.speaker: Matthew O'Brien
paras: Just wanted to start off with the guide for the full year. I think what you're -- I just want to make sure I'm clear on this. The guide actually would have gone up slightly if not for the diabetes impact of 20 basis points. So first of all, is that the right way of viewing it? 7.45% to 7.95%, something like that versus the 7.25% to 7.75% you're sticking with? And then how are you accounting for the new competition in focal catheters in the CAS franchise as you go forward, given how strong Sphere-9 has been over the last couple of years?

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: You want me to take -- I'll take the growth calculation, you're absolutely right. So the separation of MiniMed is about 20 basis points on a full year basis, about 25 basis points for the second half of the year. So you're absolutely right. The fact that we maintain the guidance is actually calling up, excluding the impact of our Diabetes consolidation.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Okay, Matt. And on the question on Afib ablation, first of all, I'm sure we'll get more questions on this. CAS continues to separate itself and firmly establish itself, our Affera platform, as the premier platform in the space. That being said you get competition coming in, as you mentioned, and you asked about the dual-energy catheters coming in from 2 of our competitors. First of all, they're just -- they're smaller tips. And I think that our larger tip is a big advantage for us. And on top of that, we're not seeing the workflow efficiencies either. So they are taking share, but not from us.

They're taking it from the third competitor. So that -- you see that reflected in our growth. We grew multiple times the market this quarter, Q2. And in Q3, we're forecasting to grow like 2.5 -- 4x actually the market in Q3 and the remainder of the year, like 2.5x the market.

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: It's -- yes, just to be clear, it's -- going forward, it's 2.5x the market on the full year, 4x the market rate. So again, in Q2, we were multiple times. We had guided to 3x. We're significantly above that. So the business is performing extremely well.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: All right. Great. Thanks, Matt. Our next question comes from Travis Steed at BofA.

segments.speaker: Travis Steed
paras: I guess, Thierry, on gross margin expansion, you've talked a lot about kind of the ability to, over time, get back to pre-COVID gross margins. And now it's part of the executive comp plan. Just maybe kind of walk through some of the early things you can do on gross margin expansion and confidence that you can kind of grow high single-digit EPS growth and especially as you comp the extra week this year?

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Sure. So look, we'll talk a lot about that during the Investor Day that we have coming up in December. But look, I think a couple of things I would say. One is -- as you can see in this quarter, we're continuing to have pretty good discipline on the pricing front. So we were up another 20 basis points this quarter, and that's despite having lapped some of the key product launches last year. So we continue to perform strongly. From a just cost-out perspective, gross cost out is hovering between 1.5% and 2% a year now, which is great. And these impacts are being offset by pressure coming from mix.

One of the pressure points used to be Diabetes. So obviously, we won't have that on a go-forward basis, which is good news. The second one is the CAS business. And as I've said many times, whereas it's kind of a short-term pressure on our gross margin level, it's actually accretive at the operating margin level. And it's the reflection of us building the installed base of mapping equipment that is going to generate the pull-through in catheters going forward. So that's good news going forward as well. This quarter, we had a little bit more pressure coming from TAVR and neuromodulation volume. But as you could see, we continue to make progress from a rate perspective versus the consensus.

So in a Kaizen fashion, adding pricing discipline to cost out, we're able to get between sort of 70 and 80 basis points of gross margin improvement. And as the mix headwinds start to get smaller, we'll see that come up to the surface in a more clear fashion. On top of that, and we'll talk about it during the Investor Day, we're taking a hard look at how we can design the products with a better cost position from the get-go. So instead of trying to get cost out from the products during the life cycle, the focus of the team is to involve the suppliers and involve engineering more upfront in product development so that we can launch them with a better margin profile.

That takes a little bit more time, but that's what ultimately will drive the real difference from a margin expansion perspective. So look, the North Star hasn't changed. You mentioned back to pre-COVID levels. It's not going to happen overnight, but that's what we're going after, and we'll keep doing that. From a leveraged earnings perspective, look, with the guidance that we gave for this year, operating margin should be up 80 to 90 basis points. There's about 40 basis points of help coming from the diabetes separation in there. But operationally, we are delivering margin expansion this year. And from an EPS perspective, at the midpoint, the guidance calls for an EPS that's up roughly 8%. So we're moving in the right direction here.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Our next question comes from Vijay Kumar at Evercore.

segments.speaker: Vijay Kumar
paras: Congrats on a nice print this morning. Geoff, on a high level on your top line rate, when you look at the 6.5% performance and you're guiding to 5% in 3Q, can you help us draw a bridge? Is that step down mostly driven by CAS? What are you assuming for any of the other segments? And I guess, is the implication now Medtronic now a sustainable 5-plus company as you comp against tougher CAS growth numbers?

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Look, thanks for the question. As -- I'm going to pivot this to Thierry in a second. But as we already talked about earlier, the guide in the second half of the year, a piece of it is due to -- on the top line that is, right? The piece of it is due to MiniMed going away, diabetes going away. And then another piece is due to a little bit of market softness we're seeing in China from VBP, particularly in our Neurovascular business. But those would be the 2 pieces. I'll turn it over to Thierry.

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Sure. Thanks for the question, Vijay. A couple of things I would add to what Geoff said. First, the comps are getting stronger in the second half, right? So we were -- in Q2 of last year, we were up 5.5%, then Q3, Q4 went 6% and 6.6%. So the comps are getting a little tougher. So the other element, as Geoff mentioned, is the deconsolidation of diabetes is about 25 basis points per quarter of organic growth. If you compare kind of the stacked growth over 2 years, you'll see that Q3 is a little softer. That's always the case. We're always -- Q3 is always the toughest for us. And on a stacked basis, Q4 gets back to kind of the second quarter kind of rhythm.

Going through the portfolio, look, Cardiovascular was up 10.4% this quarter. It's going to continue to be strong, but not quite at the same level. Two drivers. One is CAS basically because of stronger comps. One, we grew last year, 70% in the second quarter, 80% in the third quarter, and it's a bigger number. So the comps do get a little tougher. But we have super confidence in that business going forward, as Geoff mentioned.

The second one in the cardiovascular portfolio is CRM. So in CRM in the second half, we're lapping the launch of OmniaSecure. So we're going to continue to see great performance, but not quite at the same level as what we saw in the first and second quarter.

Neuroscience should be about stable for the rest of the year compared to what we saw in the first half. We continue to have great performance, in particular in CST. And what's driving that is a lot of neurosurgery with Stealth AXiS. So Stealth AXiS is performing significantly ahead of our expectations and generating pull-through in the rest of the business. And then you should expect Med-Surg to be roughly in line for the third quarter with the second quarter and the first quarter with surgery continuing to pick up, in particular, driven by robotics.

And Surgical -- Med-Surg will go down a little bit in the fourth quarter because the comps get a lot stronger, in particular, in the ACM business. So great performance from Cardiovascular, a little bit lower due to CAS and CRM and pretty similar in Neuroscience and Med-Surg in the second half versus what you've seen in the first half.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Thanks, Vijay. Larry Biegelsen is up next from Wells Fargo.

segments.speaker: Larry Biegelsen
paras: Geoff, you're hosting your first Investor Day in 6 years in a couple of weeks. Can you please give us a high-level overview of what we can expect? And Thierry, I know it's early, but could you help us think about the puts and takes for fiscal 2028 on the P&L, given the headwinds from the extra week and the tariff refunds and the Diabetes spin? Should we be thinking about kind of mid-single-digit EPS growth next year?

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: All right. Thanks for the question, Larry. Look, we're really excited about Investor Day. It's a great venue as well at the IRCAD facility. You're going to see firsthand the building blocks of our growth going forward, right? So obviously, the -- our revenues accelerated here over the last couple of quarters, building off that solid mid-single-digit growth that we had in the last couple of years. But this is the building blocks for going forward and how we see it. You're going to get to also meet a lot of the other executives behind this growth and get to talk to them, and you're going to get to see a lot of the technology live there.

Another focus is going to be how we're going to drive leveraged earnings going forward. And we'll get into that in depth. So that's what you can expect, right? The growth building blocks. There will be some new things we'll talk about there and then how we're driving that leveraged earnings. And then you get a chance to see the technology live. Anything you'd add there?

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: So on the numbers and the puts and takes for next year, at the revenue level, there will be an impact from the nonrecurrence of the 53rd week. So that -- we'll have to take that into consideration. On the flip side, though, as I mentioned in the commentary, this year, we'll have about $175 million of inorganic growth coming from Scientia, SPR and the acquisitions that we've made recently. All of these are in markets that performed significantly faster than the rest of the portfolio. And these will flip to organic in the first quarter of next year. So we'll have good news coming from that front.

At the EPS level, there will be an impact of the nonrecurrence of the 53rd week, as you mentioned. We will also have the nonrecurrence of some tariff refunds. On the flip side, we've been doing a lot of investment to grow the business going forward. And I think you should anticipate that investment in overhead to reduce a little bit and us start capitalizing more on these growth areas. So lots of puts and takes, but we'll talk more about that in detail when we get to the Investor Day. But for the guidance for '28, you're going to have to wait until May.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Next question comes from Patrick Wood at UBS.

segments.speaker: Patrick Andrew Wood
paras: I have a nerdy CRM one, but I'm going to save that for the Investor Day. So maybe more a little high level. Geoff and Thierry, both of you mentioned seeing pockets of strength, pockets of a little bit of softness here and there, and you touched the hospital in a lot of different places. So I guess the question is, what are you hearing from your customers at the hospital level around procedures, capital appetite, that sort of thing? And are you noticing any kind of differential between the U.S. customer base and OUS, ex-China because I know that has its own dynamics?

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Well, thanks, Patrick. Look, I'd say, first of all, our feedback comes from our market exposure. And right now, as benefiting from our capital allocation strategy, we're in good markets. We're in good segments, high-growth segments where clinical and technology differentiation matters and is getting rewarded even in a market like today. So we're -- overall, we're seeing pretty strong procedural growth, like I said, in innovation getting rewarded. I highlighted a few segments on the fringe of Medtronic or on the edges, I'd say, feeling pressure like spinal cord stimulation. I mentioned, globally, VBP in China.

We see China going forward here as a mid -- low to mid-single-digit grower and an important market for us, but it can be choppy quarter-to-quarter. And we already mentioned in the back half of the year, our Neurovascular business getting a VBP and a few others as well. But -- so those are the pockets where we're seeing, I'd say, softness. But overall, like strong procedure growth and hospitals are investing still.

Like take -- Thierry mentioned our Spine business, our CST business, and we're seeing Stealth AXiS exceed our expectations. Part of it is -- a big part of it is because of the differentiated technology, and that is the path forward in spine is this enabling technology being the differentiator. But it also is a strong signal that hospitals are investing. This technology is not inexpensive, and they're investing in their spine business. And when you talk to a hospital C-suite, they view like in this case, spine as a profit -- a growth and profit driver for them going forward. We can go segment by segment. But overall, those are -- that's the type of commentary that we're seeing and hearing. I don't know. Anything you'd add to that?

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: No, I think you said everything, Geoff.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Great. Next question comes from Josh Jennings at TD.

segments.speaker: Joshua Jennings
paras: Geoff and Thierry, I wanted to just circle back on your comments around China and some neurovascular VBP pressure. Any chance you can just give us some more kind of broader view on China in the back half of '27 here and into '28, any headwinds and tailwinds. And then second question, sorry to add another one in. But just was curious about Medtronic's outlook for the TAVR market growth in the setting of an unlock of the moderate AS indication. How are you guys thinking about market growth, U.S. and global?

And can Evolut maintain share and then grow at the market rate as we move through these next couple of quarters? I think you've got a 7-year low-risk data and a full set coming up within the next 6 months as well as 4-year SMART trial data [indiscernible] approved towards the Evolut franchise in the interventional cardiology community.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Maybe I'll let Thierry give you the quantification of the China VBP. But regarding Neurovascular, first, I do want to say this massive underlying neurovascular growth that we're seeing in the U.S., that business is in a really, really excited about that business and the spot that it's in. The Scientia acquisition with the really differentiated access catheter that physicians love is -- and it's disrupting the competitor there. It's had a longtime lead in this space. And it's in and of itself, it's driving a lot of growth, but it's also driving pull-through, right?

Once you get into that case on the access, it's pulling through our other ischemic and hemorrhagic products. So the business is doing really well. We're seeing strong growth in the U.S., but the China VBP is muting the global growth a bit. I'll let Thierry talk about that.

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Look, we've had VBP across the business, almost every franchise now in China, and we're having a second wave coming in neurovascular, but at lower levels than what we've experienced in the past. So it is a headwind for the business, but we're not talking impacts that are anywhere near what we experienced in the prior rounds.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: In TAVR, look, we're seeing good market growth there as well. We expect that to continue. And for Medtronic, look, we're continuing to invest around Evolut and shift the company from more of an Evolut self-expanding TAVR to a broader Structural Heart business. You saw the -- I'm guessing you saw the data that came out of London on Sunday on Anteris. That's one of our strategic investments.

We invested in Anteris based on the promise of a really compelling balloon expandable short valve, and that data is being really well received and is exciting for us. And we're continuing to invest around our Evolut platform. You've seen other investments in like Pi-Cardia, for example, and some other technologies around it. So we're excited about the end market, continuing to see good growth, and we're continuing to invest around our Evolut platform. And then from Evolut itself, we're seeing the results, the business has stabilized. Like we said, it's stabilized over the last couple of quarters, and we're moving forward.

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Yes. I would just add on TAVR that we'll lap the news on the 7-year low risk in the fourth quarter. So actually, if you look into 2028, it's one of the elements that's less of a headwind than it used to be. But going forward, the key thing, as Geoff mentioned, is we're investing in that business. And we count on a market growth that's kind of mid- to high single digits for the overall TAVR market.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: All right. Great. Next question comes from Pito Chickering at Deutsche.

segments.speaker: Pito Chickering
paras: Two questions, and I'll ask them upfront on RDN. First one is, can you talk about the Spyral and like AFFIRM study that came out and the feedback you're hearing from both implanting as well as referring physicians. And then can you talk about the transradial access and your views around how that could impact adoption and remind us the difference of procedure times between transradial and transfemoral [indiscernible].

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: So thanks, Pito. Look, first on the Spyral AFFIRM data, I mean, very, very encouraging. A couple of things I'd say there. This is at 6 months, so pretty quick response. And what it shows is that Symplicity works on a broad set of patients. So not just men but women as well, black and Hispanic populations, patients above 65 and older, type 2 diabetes patients, patients with reduced kidney function. So basically, it's saying that this works across a broad range of patients and the impact is dramatic, right?

18-point systolic blood pressure drop that we're seeing in office. And I think it's like a 10 point -- it is a 10-point in ambulatory. These -- and this is in the real world, right? A lot of times, these clinical trials are in the best case scenarios. In this case, out in the -- and they don't translate to the real world. In this case, it's translating to the real world on a broad base with a much bigger impact than I think anybody expected no matter how you measure it. And 9 out of 10 patients -- so that people are asking about what's the responder rate out in the real world at scale, 9 out of 10 patients are seeing that meaningful clinical benefit at 6 months.

And then we've already shown you last year, the 3-year data and this RF technology has sustained blood pressure reduction, even improves over time. And we've got all kinds of data no matter how you slice it. So really -- I mean, really excited about this. And I stand by my comments for the last couple of years. I think this is going to be the biggest thing we've ever done when you look back on it. And then finally, on transradial, it is -- we moved to transradial in the second half of our fiscal year here, FY '27.

And it is meaningfully faster and easier. I don't have the quantification of how much the time savings, I don't have it off the top of my head, but it's meaningfully -- I know that it's -- and physicians are really excited about it. And the theme here is as we're developing the market, which is what we're doing now and getting out there with referral pathways and making sure everybody understands the economics of it. In parallel, we continue to invest in the efficacy of the product. I just -- the therapy, I just walked through the clinical data and the diversity of it, the high responder rate.

But we're also investing in the product itself and the procedure itself to make it faster and easier. At the end of the day, we want to make sure -- and then pretty soon, you're going to start to see the branding that we're going to do and building up a brand here. We're making sure that we're multiple generations of anybody coming after us because we're doing a lot of work to develop the market, and we want to maintain that lead. So when you look at the revenue, we're seeing growth. But quite frankly, it hasn't inflected yet. But it's not a question of if, it's a question of when. And we couldn't be more -- all of the leading indicators are super positive on this, and we're really excited.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Our next question comes from Robbie Marcus at JPMorgan.

segments.speaker: Robert Marcus
paras: Thierry, it's sort of a quick informational 2-part question. One, now that MiniMed has been spun out, how do we think about what underlying margins are for the business, gross and operating margin? Perhaps you could give us the historical for third, fourth and full year? And then within that, how do we think about what the TSA revenues are? How large are they? And when do they go through?

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Robbie, so on the impact on margin, we had said previously on a full year basis, the MiniMed was kind of dilutive by roughly 50 basis points at the gross margin level and 90 to 100 basis points at the operating margin level. So we'll get a portion of that benefit in the second half of this year. And you'll see that primarily in the operating margin. So as I said, for full year operating margin this year, we should be up 80 to 90 basis points and roughly half of that comes from MiniMed. So that's what to have in mind. And then on the TSA revenue, what you should have in mind is roughly $50 million a quarter, and that will continue until sort of the end of fiscal year '28 and gradually go down as we sort of exit these agreements and MiniMed starts doing everything on their own.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Great. Next question comes from Anthony Petrone at Mizuho.

segments.speaker: Anthony Petrone
paras: Maybe 2 quick product questions. One would just be on Hugo, in the prepared materials, you're sticking with the guidance here for 50,000 global procedures. I'm just wondering as we sit here in late November here looking at Thanksgiving, how the funnel for capital looks maybe into the end of the year and into early 2027. And then on renal denervation, great data out there, Geoff, that you highlighted. You also referenced the Cat I code that becomes effective January 2028. Do you think that cycle to see an inflection is more dependent on the data here or that Cat I code kicking in, in January 2028?

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Thanks, Anthony. Let me start with the RDN question, and I'm kicking myself. I forgot to mention the Cat I code. That's a big one. I got carried away with the product itself. Obviously, you can see my enthusiasm. But the Cat I code is a big deal and a bigger deal than I even thought. One, it's an increase effectively in reimbursement. This one is focused on how the physicians get compensated.

But more than that, what it does is it is an indicator to payers that the therapy is here to stay and not an investigative therapy. And what -- more than 20%, almost 30% of the payers look at a therapy without Cat I as investigative. And now that we've got that Cat I code, the conversations with payers, and I had a breakfast meeting with a large payer just the other day, have changed and accelerated.

We were making pretty good progress even without this. But now we expect things to accelerate with the commercial payers and the covered lives to improve. So the Cat I code is a big one. And we also got it this quarter with Altaviva, same story there is that's going to really drive covered lives for us. And then on Hugo, yes, the pipeline looks good. We're still on track for -- to deliver over 250 global installs by the end of the fiscal year on a cumulative basis. So we're starting to get a good-sized installed base.

And now that we've got in the U.S. that general surgery indication, that dramatically increases the number of procedures we can cover. I think the general surgery is like 60% of the overall procedures, and now we got that covered. So it makes the Hugo more of a workhorse platform for hospitals. And I think that's going to have -- I know that's going to have a meaningful impact on the acceleration of our installed base. We've had a lot of physician interest in it. And sometimes you get to the C-suite and they say, well, we'll pull the trigger once we see a broader case coverage here. So the general surgery was the biggest piece of it. So it's really important for us.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Thanks, Anthony. Next question comes from Mike Kratky at Leerink.

segments.speaker: Michael Kratky
paras: Can you just provide an update on where things stand for Sphere-360, both in terms of when we could see those top line results from the U.S. trial, potential launch timing in the U.S. and just on the status of OUS commercialization?

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: So on 360, we just completed, Mike, the trial enrollment. And so now we'll submit that to -- we have a 12-month follow-up from the trial enrollment, right? And then we submit it -- we have a little bit of an analysis period. It's not long, and then we submit it to the FDA. And I think that can take up to 6 months time frame.

So we got a 12-month follow-up and then we have the submission to the FDA, which is probably around -- we're estimating around 6 months. So that's where we are on 360 in the U.S. And in Europe, look, we've gotten really, really good feedback on the therapy there. It's very effective. The workflow is great, just like Sphere-9 and it's lightning fast, lightning fast and it's easy to use. So feedback really positive, which I think bodes well for Europe, but also for what we're going to see in the U.S. once this therapy comes on the market. And remember, it goes right at our main competitor in the space. So I think that also bodes well for our continuation of share gains and growth.

segments.speaker: Ingrid Goldberg
paras: Thanks, Mike. I think we have time for one more. So we'll take it from Ryan Zimmerman at BTIG.

segments.speaker: Ryan Zimmerman
paras: I'll end on a note on Spine actually. So it grew -- CST grew about 6.1% organically in 2Q, but we did note around 13% in Q1. And so Geoff, just to -- as we think about those dynamics, the step down, is that a combination of tough comps, maybe distributor conversions on ModuLeX and just underlying volume softness? And just is mid-single digits the right run rate for core spine going forward?

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: I'll have Thierry answer some of the growth questions there. But I'd say on spine, we're seeing really strong adoption of Stealth AXiS. And it's for a number of reasons. One, it is just an improved functionality of the robot itself. But the big one is the workflow. It allows -- 70% of the cases in the U.S., which is by far the biggest market for spine are navigated. And the Stealth AXiS is built around the navigation workflow.

So for those 70% of the cases of people that -- which is a leading indicator of those surgeons that are leaning into enabling technology, it's a much easier next step to go into robotics. And up to now, that hasn't been the case with our technology or our competitors. So now we have that seamless workflow and an improved robot. And so we're seeing really a lot of growth. We're seeing hospitals invest in the Spine business. And if there's like a procedural slowdown in spine, we're not really feeling that.
But I'll let Thierry talk about the difference in numbers from the quarter.

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Yes. Just in the first quarter, we were up, I think, 13%, but that included the extra week, right? So if you correct on that, it was around 6%. It's around 6% this quarter again. So that's kind of the run rate. So mid- to high single digits, I would say.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: The last thing I'll say, Ryan, on this point is this adoption of the enabling technology and the improvements of the enabling technology, the features of it and the dramatic improvements of the workflow has really changed the competitive dynamics and the competitive set has dramatically narrowed. And with us leading, we feel like we're in a really good spot now, but durably into the future.

segments.speaker: Thierry Pieton
paras: Look, I was looking at some market share data. If you look at first quarter of '24 in CST in total, we had about 30% market share. Now we're at 38%. So that business is really performing well.

segments.speaker: Geoffrey Martha
paras: Okay. All right. Well, thank you, all of you for joining, and I appreciate the support, the continued support and the interest in Medtronic. And I want to wish for those that are celebrating, have a great Thanksgiving, and I apologize for having this call on Thanksgiving week, but -- and have a great rest of your day. Thank you.
